hints.problem_summary: Missing semicolon at the end of a variable declaration statement.
hints.why: In Java, every statement must end with a semicolon (;). The compiler needs this to know where one statement ends and another begins. Without it, the compiler gets confused and reports a syntax error.

hints.learning_tip: Always ensure string literals are properly enclosed in double quotes and escape special characters when needed.
hints.problem_summary: The string literal is missing a closing quotation mark.
hints.why: In Java, string literals must be enclosed in matching quotation marks. The compiler expects a closing quote to complete the string, but it's missing.

hints.why: In Java, every opening brace '{' must have a corresponding closing brace '}'. The for loop starts a block of code that needs to be properly closed before the main method ends.

hints.hint_1: Look at the data type of your variable and compare it to the value you're trying to assign.

hints.problem_summary: The student is trying to assign a string value to an integer variable.
hints.why: In Java, variables have specific data types that determine what kind of values they can hold. An int variable can only store whole numbers, not text strings. The compiler prevents this type mismatch to avoid runtime errors.

hints.learning_tip: Read about variable declaration and initialization in Java, and the concept of 'forward reference' errors.
hints.problem_summary: The variable 'result' is used before it is declared.
hints.why: In Java, variables must be declared before they can be used. The compiler reads the code from top to bottom and doesn't know what 'result' means when it encounters it on line 3.

hints.hint_3: The correct method name is 'length()' - try calling text.length() instead.
hints.learning_tip: Method names in Java must be spelled exactly as defined in the API documentation. Always double-check spelling and capitalization when getting 'cannot find symbol' errors.
hints.problem_summary: The student misspelled the method name 'length()' as 'lenght()'.
hints.why: Java is case-sensitive and requires exact method names. The String class has a method called 'length()' that returns the number of characters, but 'lenght()' doesn't exist.

hints.problem_summary: The array declaration mixes integers and a string value.
hints.why: An int array can only store integer values, but the code tries to store a string "three" in the third position. Java is strongly typed, so this type mismatch causes a compilation error.

hints.learning_tip: Review the correct syntax for for loops in Java, specifically the use of semicolons as separators.
hints.problem_summary: The for loop uses commas instead of semicolons to separate its components.
hints.why: In Java, the for loop syntax requires three parts separated by semicolons: initialization, condition, and increment. Using commas causes the compiler to misinterpret the syntax structure.

hints.hint_1: Look at what value the 'text' variable holds when you try to use it.

hints.learning_tip: Learn about null references and how to handle them safely using null checks or Optional classes.
hints.problem_summary: The code tries to call a method on a null reference.
hints.why: When a variable is null, it doesn't point to any actual object in memory. Calling methods on null references causes a NullPointerException because there's no object to execute the method on.

hints.why: Arrays in Java have a fixed size once created. The array 'arr' has only 3 elements at indices 0, 1, and 2, but the code attempts to access index 5 which is beyond the array's bounds.

hints.hint_1: Look at the factorial method and think about when the recursion should stop.

hints.problem_summary: The factorial method causes infinite recursion leading to a stack overflow.
hints.why: The recursive method lacks a base case to stop the recursion. It keeps calling itself indefinitely, consuming stack memory until it overflows.

hints.hint_1: Look at the values of your variables when performing mathematical operations.
hints.hint_2: Check what value you're using as the denominator in your division operation and make sure it's not zero.
hints.hint_3: Before dividing, add a condition to check if the divisor equals zero, for example: `if (b != 0) { System.out.println(a / b); }`
hints.learning_tip: Learn about exception handling in Java using try-catch blocks to handle runtime errors gracefully.
hints.problem_summary: Division by zero causes an ArithmeticException at runtime.
hints.why: In mathematics, division by zero is undefined, and Java throws an ArithmeticException when this operation is attempted. The error occurs because the variable 'b' is initialized to 0 and used as the divisor.

hints.hint_1: Look at what type of object is stored in the 'obj' variable and compare it to what you're trying to cast it to.
hints.hint_2: You need to ensure that the object you're casting actually represents the type you're casting to, or use a different approach to convert between types.

hints.learning_tip: Research the difference between casting objects and converting between data types in Java, including wrapper classes and their conversion methods.
hints.problem_summary: The code attempts to cast a String object to an Integer, which causes a ClassCastException.
hints.why: In Java, you cannot cast an object to a type that it doesn't actually represent. The variable 'obj' contains a String value 'Hello', but the code tries to force it into an Integer type, which is incompatible.

hints.why: Strings in Java are zero-indexed, meaning the first character is at index 0. The string 'Java' has only 4 characters, so valid indices are 0, 1, 2, and 3. Trying to access index 10 goes beyond the string's length.

hints.why: When you create a Scanner with a string like "hello", it treats that string as the input source. Since "hello" is not a number, calling nextInt() causes an InputMismatchException because the scanner cannot convert the text to an integer.

hints.problem_summary: The program attempts to create an array with a negative size, which is not allowed in Java.
hints.why: In Java, arrays must have a non-negative size because they represent a fixed number of elements in memory. When you try to create an array with a negative size, the JVM throws a NegativeArraySizeException at runtime.

hints.why: In Java, variables declared inside a block (like an if statement) are only accessible within that block. Once the block ends, the variable goes out of scope and cannot be accessed anymore.

hints.problem_summary: The student is trying to use the equals() method on a primitive int variable.
hints.why: Primitive data types like int don't have methods - they are not objects. The equals() method belongs to the Integer class, not the int primitive type. When you try to call a method on a primitive, Java doesn't know what object to call it on.

hints.problem_summary: The greet() method returns void but is being assigned to a String variable.
hints.why: In Java, methods with a void return type don't produce a value that can be stored in a variable. When you try to assign the result of a void method to a variable, the compiler doesn't know what value to use since void means 'no return value'.

results.description: Accessing private member from another context

hints.hint_1: Look at the access modifier of the 'name' field in the Animal class.
hints.hint_2: Consider providing a public method in the Animal class that returns the value of the private field.

hints.learning_tip: Learn about encapsulation and access modifiers (private, public, protected, default) in Java classes.
hints.problem_summary: The code tries to access a private field from outside its class.
hints.why: In Java, private fields can only be accessed within the same class where they are declared. The 'name' field in the Animal class is private, so it cannot be accessed directly from the Main class.

hints.hint_1: Look at the relationship between your main method and the display method.
hints.hint_2: Consider how you can make the display method accessible from the static main method.

hints.learning_tip: Study the difference between static and non-static methods and when to use each.
hints.problem_summary: The static main method is trying to call a non-static method directly.
hints.why: In Java, static methods belong to the class itself, while non-static methods belong to instances of the class. Static methods cannot directly access non-static methods because there's no instance to call them on.

hints.problem_summary: The code tries to add a String to an ArrayList that only accepts Integer objects.
hints.why: The ArrayList is declared to hold only Integer objects, so when you try to add a String like "three", Java's type safety prevents this incompatible assignment. Generic types in Java enforce that only the specified type can be added to the collection.
